idea: Browser extension that reads any webpage aloud in the voice of a historical figure the user picks, using a small on-device text-to-speech model, no cloud calls, free tier limited to 10 minutes per day.
note: Top-level cut only (one pass, not recursed to atomic) -- this is a scoping comparison of how differently each Slicer variant divides the SAME idea, not five full trees. Hand-authored by Claude Sonnet 5, same session as tools/slicer.yaml.

binary-halving.text: The technical half: an on-device TTS model exists, runs inside browser-extension audio APIs, at acceptable latency.
The adoption half: voice rights clear, users find it more than a novelty, and the free tier converts to paid.

thirds.text: An on-device TTS model exists and runs inside browser-extension audio APIs at acceptable latency.
Historical-figure voice packs can be produced or licensed without infringing likeness or IP rights.
Users find it more than a novelty, and a 10-minute/day free tier converts to paid.

variants.by-layer: same as problems/voice-extension.json's 5 pieces (tts-model, extension-audio, voice-rights, product-appeal, conversion) -- this variant is what that file already does by hand

by-risk.text: A licensable, on-device TTS model exists for this use case at all.

Everything else (extension audio integration, voice rights, product appeal, conversion), assumed answerable once the TTS-model risk resolves favorably -- itself re-cut by this same rule on the next pass.

by-phase.text: Spike: does a licensable on-device TTS model exist, and can it run inside browser-extension audio APIs.
Decide: which historical figures/voices to launch with, given rights constraints.
Build: the extension itself -- TTS integration, voice picker, the free-tier timer.
Validate: do users keep using it past the novelty, and does the free tier actually convert.
Launch: ship the free tier with an upgrade path.

finding: All five CAN slice this idea -- that part of the question is settled. What differs is what falls out the other end: binary-halving/thirds (2-3 pieces) are the coarsest, closest to how a person actually starts, but need the most Grinder passes before anything is atomic enough to be a requirement. by-risk (2 pieces) front-loads prioritization into the tree shape itself, at the cost of being lopsided and hard to map onto a schedule. by-layer and by-phase (5 pieces each) are the two that already produce something requirement-shaped in one pass: by-layer is what problems/*.json already do and is proven against live Bouncer/Weigher; by-phase is the one that maps directly onto 'a standard development window' since it reuses lab_decompose.py's own phase taxonomy and could plug straight into the existing CPM machinery. Tentative conclusion: by-layer and by-phase look like the two worth taking further; binary-halving/thirds/by-risk are real but better suited as an outer loop that decides *when* to switch layers/phases, not as the primary cut.
